items.stem: Reading the scale of a measuring instrument from an angle rather than square on introduces

misconception.label: A zero error comes from the instrument itself, not from where the eye is.

items.stem: A measuring instrument reads 0.3 cm when nothing is placed in it. This is an example of

misconception.label: A random error scatters readings; this one is the same every time.

items.stem: A solid block is cut exactly in half. Compared with the whole block, each half has

misconception.label: Halving the mass alone would halve the density, but the volume halves too.
Neither the mass nor the volume falls to a quarter.
Nothing about cutting a block makes it denser.

steps: Density is ρ = m / V.
Cutting the block in half halves the mass and halves the volume.
Halving the top and the bottom of a fraction leaves it unchanged, so each half has the same density as the whole. Density is a property of the substance, not of how much of it there is.

items.stem: Which quantity is a vector?

misconception.label: Mass is a scalar; a body has the same mass whichever way it faces.
Energy is a scalar; it has no direction.
Time is a scalar.

steps: A vector has both magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only.
Acceleration says how quickly the velocity changes and in what direction.
Mass, energy and time all have size alone.

items.objective_statement: use scale diagrams to find the resultant of two vectors
items.stem: Two forces of 5 N and 3 N act on a body at the same point. The resultant CANNOT be

misconception.label: 8 N is the sum, obtained when the forces act in the same direction.
2 N is the difference, obtained when they act in opposite directions.
4 N lies between 2 N and 8 N and is obtained at a suitable angle.

steps: Forces in the same direction give the largest resultant, 5 + 3 = 8 N.
Forces in opposite directions give the smallest, 5 − 3 = 2 N.
Every angle in between gives a resultant somewhere between 2 N and 8 N, so 10 N is impossible.

items.stem: Two forces of 5 N and 3 N act at a point in opposite directions. The magnitude of their resultant, in N, is

misconception.label: That would be the resultant if the forces were at right angles.

steps: The two forces act along the same straight line.
Acting in opposite directions, they partly cancel.
The resultant is 5 − 3 = 2 N, in the direction of the larger force.

is a vector while weight is a scalar

items.objective_statement: show how derived quantities and their related units are produced
items.stem: Which quantity is NOT a base quantity in the SI system?

misconception.label: Length is a base quantity, measured in metres.
Time is a base quantity, measured in seconds.
Electric current is a base quantity, measured in amperes.

steps: A base quantity is one the system defines directly rather than building from others.
Force comes from F = ma, which uses mass, length and time.
So force is derived, and the newton is a derived unit equal to kg m s⁻².

items.stem: The SI base unit of mass is the

misconception.label: The gram is a submultiple of the base unit, not the base unit itself.

items.stem: Joule's experiments were important because they established that

options.text: heat is a fluid stored in bodies

misconception.label: That is the caloric theory Joule's work helped to overturn.

options.text: a fixed amount of mechanical work always produces the same amount of heat

misconception.label: Net flow is always from hot to cold.

options.text: temperature and thermal energy are the same thing

misconception.label: The two are different: temperature says how hot, thermal energy says how much.

steps: Joule stirred water with paddles driven by falling weights and measured the temperature rise.
Whatever the arrangement, the same amount of work always gave the same amount of heating.
That fixed ratio meant work was being converted into thermal energy, not that some fluid was being released.
solution.answer_line: a fixed amount of mechanical work always produces the same amount of heat

options.text: bring up a negative rod, earth the sphere, remove the rod, remove the earth

stimulus.alt: A graph of current against potential difference for a semiconductor diode. In the reverse direction the current is almost zero; in the forward direction it stays near zero until about 0.7 volts and then rises steeply.

items.stem: The graph shows that the diode

options.text: obeys Ohm's law in both directions

misconception.label: Ohm's law would give a straight line through the origin, which this is not.
A constant resistance would give a straight line; the gradient changes sharply.

options.text: conducts equally well in both directions

misconception.label: The two branches are completely different, which is the point of the graph.

options.text: conducts in one direction only, and then only above a small potential difference

steps: Look at the reverse half: the current stays almost zero however large the reverse voltage.
Look at the forward half: the current is also almost zero until about 0.7 V, and then rises steeply.
So the diode conducts one way only, and only once the forward voltage is large enough. Its resistance is not constant, so it does not obey Ohm's law.
solution.answer_line: conducts in one direction only, and then only above a small potential difference

misconception.label: Separated humps are the rectifier output, not the battery.

options.text: a curve crossing the axis regularly

options.text: a line rising steadily with time

steps: Sketch voltage against time for each.

A half wave rectifier gives humps above the axis with gaps where the reverse half cycles were blocked.

items.objective_statement: distinguish between materials used to make "permanent" and "temporary" magnets
items.stem: A magnetically hard material is one that is

options.text: easy to magnetise and easy to demagnetise

misconception.label: That describes a magnetically soft material such as soft iron.

options.text: unable to be magnetised at all

misconception.label: A magnetically hard material can certainly be magnetised; it just takes more effort.

options.text: easy to magnetise and hard to demagnetise

misconception.label: No common material behaves this way.

options.text: hard to magnetise and hard to demagnetise

steps: The words hard and soft here describe magnetic behaviour, not physical hardness.
A magnetically soft material such as soft iron magnetises easily and loses it at once, which suits an electromagnet core.
A magnetically hard material such as steel takes more effort to magnetise but then keeps it, which is what a permanent magnet needs.
solution.answer_line: hard to magnetise and hard to demagnetise

options.text: cutting a magnet always produces two complete magnets with two poles each
north poles do not exist on their own

misconception.label: This restates the conclusion rather than explaining it.

options.text: the Earth's field would cancel it

misconception.label: The Earth's field does not cancel anything.

options.text: the magnet would lose its magnetism

misconception.label: Cutting a magnet does not destroy its magnetism.

steps: Cut a bar magnet in half and each half is a complete magnet.
New poles appear at the cut faces, so each piece has a north and a south.
Repeating the cut always gives the same result, so a single pole cannot be isolated.
solution.answer_line: cutting a magnet always produces two complete magnets with two poles each

stimulus.alt: A relay. A 6 volt circuit with a switch drives a coil, whose armature closes the contacts of a separate 240 volt circuit containing a lamp.

items.stem: The main reason for using a relay here is that it

options.text: reduces the current in the lamp

misconception.label: The lamp draws whatever current its resistance and the 240 V supply give it.

options.text: increases the voltage across the lamp

misconception.label: The relay does not change any voltage.

options.text: lets a small safe current switch a large dangerous one, with no electrical connection between them

misconception.label: Brightness is set by the lamp and its supply, not by the relay.

steps: Closing the switch sends a small current through the coil, which becomes an electromagnet.
The electromagnet attracts the armature, which closes the contacts of the separate 240 V circuit.
Nothing conducts between the two circuits, so the low voltage side stays safe to touch. That isolation is why a relay is used.
solution.answer_line: lets a small safe current switch a large dangerous one, with no electrical connection between them

items.objective_statement: predict the direction of induced current given the direction of motion of the conductor and that of the magnetic field
items.stem: Lenz's law says that the direction of an induced current is always such that it

options.text: increases the change that produced it

misconception.label: Reinforcing the change would make the effect grow without limit and create energy from nothing.

options.text: is at right angles to the magnetic field

misconception.label: The law is about direction relative to the change, not relative to the field.
That is the convention for conventional current in any circuit, not Lenz's law.

options.text: opposes the change that produced it

steps: Push a magnet towards a coil and a current is induced.
That current makes the coil into a magnet that pushes back against the incoming magnet.
So work has to be done to keep pushing, and that work is what becomes the electrical energy. If the coil pulled the magnet in instead, energy would appear from nowhere.
solution.answer_line: opposes the change that produced it

items.objective_statement: explain the action of the A.C. generator
items.stem: The output of a simple alternating current generator can be increased by

misconception.label: Turning more slowly reduces the rate of change of flux and so the output.

options.text: using fewer turns on the coil

misconception.label: Fewer turns give a smaller e.m.f.
A weaker field gives a smaller e.m.f.

steps: The induced e.m.f. depends on how quickly the flux linking the coil changes.
Spinning the coil faster sweeps it through the field more rapidly.
More turns and a stronger magnet also increase the output, for the same reason.

items.stem: Compared with a proton, a neutron has

options.text: about the same mass and no charge
about the same mass and an equal positive charge

options.text: a much smaller mass and no charge

misconception.label: Its mass is about the same as the proton's, not much smaller.

options.text: a much larger mass and a negative charge

misconception.label: It is neither much heavier nor negative.

steps: The proton and the neutron each have a mass of about one atomic mass unit.
The proton carries a charge of +1 and the neutron carries none.
The electron, by contrast, has about 1/1836 of that mass and a charge of −1.

items.objective_statement: explain why an atom is normally neutral and stable
items.stem: An atom has no overall charge because it contains

misconception.label: It contains protons and electrons, both of which are charged.
Neutrons carry no charge, so their number does not affect neutrality.

options.text: equal numbers of protons and electrons
equal numbers of protons and neutrons

misconception.label: The neutron number varies between isotopes without affecting the charge.

steps: A proton carries +1 and an electron carries −1.
A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons.
So the charges cancel exactly, whatever the number of neutrons.
solution.answer_line: equal numbers of protons and electrons

items.objective_statement: state the nature of the three types of radioactive emissions
items.stem: Which emission has the greatest ionising power?

misconception.label: Beta is less strongly ionising than alpha, which is why it travels further.
Gamma is the weakest ioniser, which is why it is the most penetrating.
They differ greatly; that is why their ranges differ.

steps: Ionising power and penetrating power run in opposite directions.
Alpha ionises most strongly, so it loses its energy within a few centimetres of air.
Gamma ionises weakly, so it passes through centimetres of lead before being much reduced.

items.stem: An alpha particle is identical to a

misconception.label: A hydrogen nucleus is a single proton.
A fast electron is a beta particle.

steps: Alpha decay removes two protons and two neutrons from a nucleus.
Two protons and two neutrons together make the nucleus of helium-4.
So the emitted particle is a helium nucleus with a charge of +2 and a mass number of 4.

items.stem: In carbon dating, the age of a once living sample is estimated from

misconception.label: Mass tells nothing about age.

options.text: the number of carbon atoms it contains

misconception.label: The total number of carbon atoms depends on the size of the sample, not on its age.
Colour is not related to age in this way.

options.text: the fraction of its carbon-14 that has decayed

steps: While alive, an organism exchanges carbon with its surroundings and keeps a fixed proportion of carbon-14.
At death that exchange stops and the carbon-14 decays with a half-life of about 5700 years.
Measuring what fraction is left and counting half-lives gives the time since death.
solution.answer_line: the fraction of its carbon-14 that has decayed
